intro: The show drops real anatomical and surgical eponyms into its satire almost as often as invented ones. This index is the difference: who each name really belongs to, and the moment it's said. We're adding to it as new episodes air.

entries.name: Hippocrates
entries.what: Ancient Greek physician traditionally called the father of Western medicine. The ethical tradition of the Hippocratic Oath still carries his name.

entries.name: Sigmund Freud
entries.what: Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis. His 1905 book Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious is the (real) premise behind this episode's (fictional) cure for physician burnout.

entries.name: John Bobbs and the first gallbladder operation
entries.what: Indianapolis surgeon credited with the first cholecystotomy, opening the gallbladder to remove a stone, in 1867.

entries.name: McBurney's point
entries.what: The point on the abdomen, about a third of the way from the right hip bone to the navel, where tenderness classically signals appendicitis. Described by the American surgeon Charles McBurney in 1889.

entries.name: Reginald Heber Fitz and "appendicitis"
entries.what: American pathologist who coined the term "appendicitis" in an 1886 paper and argued for removing the appendix early, a case credited with launching the modern operation.

entries.name: Connell suture
entries.what: An all-layer inverting stitch for closing the bowel, described by the American surgeon F. G. Connell.

entries.name: Lembert suture
entries.what: A stitch that turns the bowel's outer layer inward to seal an incision, described by the French surgeon Antoine Lembert in 1826 and still used today.

entries.name: Erle Peacock and wound healing
entries.what: American surgeon and researcher whose studies of collagen and scar formation, including his textbook on wound repair, shaped modern understanding of how wounds heal.

entries.name: William Halsted
entries.what: American surgeon who built the modern surgical residency at Johns Hopkins, insisting on gentle tissue handling, sterile technique and years of hands-on training before independent practice.

entries.name: William Osler
entries.what: Canadian physician and one of the four founding professors of Johns Hopkins Hospital, often called the father of modern clinical medicine for insisting students learn at the bedside.

entries.name: Hesselbach's triangle
entries.what: A triangular area of the lower abdominal wall, bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the rectus muscle and the inguinal ligament, through which a direct inguinal hernia pushes. Described by the German anatomist and surgeon Franz Kaspar Hesselbach in 1806.

entries.name: Bassini repair
entries.what: A technique for repairing inguinal hernias by reinforcing the layers of the abdominal wall, described by the Italian surgeon Edoardo Bassini in 1887. It was the standard hernia repair for most of the 20th century.

entries.name: Camper's fascia
entries.what: The outer, fattier layer of the abdominal wall's tissue beneath the skin, named for the Dutch anatomist and physician Petrus Camper.

entries.name: Scarpa's fascia
entries.what: The deeper, more fibrous layer of the abdominal wall's tissue beneath the skin, lying under Camper's fascia. Named for the Italian anatomist and surgeon Antonio Scarpa.

entries.name: Parviz Amid and the triple neurectomy
entries.what: Hernia surgeon known for popularizing the triple neurectomy, removing three groin nerves, to treat chronic pain after hernia repair, and for publishing large case series on the procedure's results.

entries.name: Mirizzi syndrome
entries.what: A gallstone lodged in the neck of the gallbladder presses on the main bile duct and causes jaundice. First described by the Argentine surgeon Pablo Luis Mirizzi in 1948.

entries.name: Ducts of Luschka
entries.what: Small accessory bile ducts that sometimes run directly from the liver into the gallbladder bed; if cut during gallbladder surgery, they can leak bile. Named for the German anatomist Hubert von Luschka.

entries.name: Charcot's triad
entries.what: Fever, jaundice and right-upper-abdominal pain together signal cholangitis, an infection of the bile ducts. Described by the French physician Jean-Martin Charcot, better known as a founder of modern neurology.

entries.name: Billroth I and II
entries.what: The Austrian surgeon who performed the first successful stomach removal for cancer in 1881; the two ways of reconnecting the digestive tract afterward still carry his name, Billroth I and Billroth II.

entries.name: Kocher maneuver
entries.what: A technique for mobilizing the duodenum to expose the structures behind it, described by the Swiss surgeon Emil Theodor Kocher, who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the thyroid gland.

entries.name: Fogarty catheter
entries.what: A thin, balloon-tipped catheter used to pull blood clots and stones out of vessels and ducts. Invented in 1961 by Thomas Fogarty, then still a surgical technician, later a prolific American surgeon-inventor.

entries.name: Ignaz Semmelweis and handwashing
entries.what: Hungarian physician who showed in 1847 that deaths from childbed fever on his maternity ward fell sharply once doctors washed their hands between the autopsy room and the delivery room. His colleagues largely dismissed him during his lifetime.

entries.name: Segura basket
entries.what: A small wire basket threaded through an endoscope to snare and pull out stones from the bile duct or urinary tract, named for the American urologist Joseph Segura.

entries.name: LaVeen shunt
entries.what: A one-way tube implanted to drain fluid from the abdomen into a vein, developed in the 1970s by the American surgeon Harry LaVeen to treat severe ascites.

entries.name: Robert Bárány and the caloric test
entries.what: Austrian-Swedish physician who won the 1914 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for working out how the inner ear's balance system reacts to hot and cold water, the basis of the caloric reflex test still used in balance clinics and coma exams.
